extracted.intended_audience: historians and philosophers of science; scientists and graduate students interested in theory change and scientific methodology
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on how scientific crises arise, how scientists respond, and how new theories/paradigms emerge; intended to identify features, behaviors, and contextual conditions that characterize paradigm change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crises as precondition for novel theories
rubrics_metrics.description: Crises are a necessary precondition for the emergence of novel theories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kuhn argues that the novel theory seems a direct response to crisis; examples include Copernicus and other historical cases where breakdown preceded the new theory’s enunciation. Except for special cases (e.g., Copernicus with external factors), breakdown and proliferation of theories typically occur a decade or two before the new theory is proposed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Breakdown typically follows long-recognized problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Problems that precipitate crisis are often long-recognized and had previously been considered solved or nearly solved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because these problems had long been viewed as solved, their eventual failure produces an acute sense of crisis; contrast with entirely new problems, which are disappointing but not surprising.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipations ignored absent crisis
rubrics_metrics.description: Solutions or anticipations of new theories, when they appear before crisis, are often ignored until crisis makes them relevant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Aristarchus’ heliocentric suggestion was ignored because Ptolemaic astronomy met contemporary needs; Copernicus later benefited from a recognized crisis. Similarly, seventeenth-century combustion theories failed to gain traction because they did not address recognized trouble spots.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiplicity of theoretical constructions on same data
rubrics_metrics.description: More than one theoretical construction can always be placed upon a given collection of data; alternates are relatively easy to invent in early/developmental stages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: History shows that inventing alternates is uncommon during normal science and tends to occur in pre-paradigm stages or special occasions during later evolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternates are seldom pursued except in pre-paradigm or crisis conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientists seldom undertake invention of alternate theoretical constructions except during the pre-paradigm stage or during special occasions (e.g., crisis).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As long as a paradigm’s tools solve the problems it defines, scientists stick with it — retooling is an extravagance reserved for appropriate occasions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paradigm rejection requires an available alternate
rubrics_metrics.description: The act of judgment that leads scientists to reject a previously accepted theory is always based upon more than a comparison of that theory with the world; a paradigm is declared invalid only if an alternate candidate is available to take its place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No historical process resembles pure falsification by direct comparison with nature; the decision to reject one paradigm is simultaneously a decision to accept another and involves comparison of both paradigms with nature and with each other.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientists do not renounce paradigms in face of anomalies
rubrics_metrics.description: Though scientists may lose faith and consider alternatives, they do not renounce the paradigm that has led them into crisis; they do not treat anomalies simply as counter-instances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical practice shows defenders devise numerous articulations and ad hoc modifications rather than abandoning the paradigm outright.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ad hoc modifications and defenses of paradigms
rubrics_metrics.description: Defenders of a paradigm confronted with anomalies will devise articulations and ad hoc modifications to eliminate apparent conflicts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many such modifications are present in the literature; counterinstances alone are usually only a minor irritant unless they permit emergence of a new analysis of science.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counterinstances alone cannot compel paradigm change
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophical or experimental counterinstances by themselves will not falsify a philosophical theory — its defenders will modify or reinterpret to absorb them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only when counterinstances help permit a new and different analysis (a new paradigm) do they become more than minor irritants; from within a new theory they may appear tautological rather than anomalous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejecting a paradigm without substituting another is rejecting science
rubrics_metrics.description: To reject one paradigm without simultaneously substituting another is to reject science itself; such an act reflects on the individual, not on the paradigm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kuhn uses metaphors like 'the carpenter who blames his tools' to indicate the social/professional consequences of abandoning paradigms without alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research necessarily presumes a paradigm
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no such thing as research in the absence of any paradigm; normal science presumes the validity of the paradigm when solving puzzles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even puzzles of normal science can be construed as counterinstances from another viewpoint; the existence of counterinstances is constant, but their interpretation depends on paradigm context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pedagogical acceptance of theory on authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Science students often accept theories on the authority of teacher and text rather than because of evidence; textbook applications are part of learning the paradigm, not evidence for it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If applications were presented as evidence, failure to show alternative interpretations would be biased; but pedagogical practice fosters acceptance by authority and exemplification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anomaly must be more than an anomaly to evoke crisis
rubrics_metrics.description: For an anomaly to evoke crisis it usually must be more than just a discrepancy; it must call into question fundamental generalizations, have practical importance, or change status as normal science develops.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: ether-drag problems threatened Maxwellian fundamentals; Copernican issues became pressing due to calendar and astrological importance; weight-relation problems became critical after pneumatic-chemical technique development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crisis begins with blurring of paradigm and loosening rules
rubrics_metrics.description: All crises begin with the blurring of a paradigm and the consequent loosening of the rules for normal research; this produces proliferation of divergent articulations or ad hoc adjustments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: With continuing resistance, many partial solutions appear, the rules become blurred, and few practitioners fully agree on what the paradigm is.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three modes of crisis closure
rubrics_metrics.description: All crises close in one of three ways: (1) normal science handles the problem and crisis passes; (2) problem resists and is set aside for a future generation; or (3) a new candidate paradigm emerges and a battle over acceptance ensues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kuhn emphasizes the third outcome (emergence of a new paradigm) as central to revolutions; later sections examine the battle over acceptance in detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transition to new paradigm is reconstruction, not cumulative extension
rubrics_metrics.description: The transition from a paradigm in crisis to a new one is a reconstruction of the field from new fundamentals, changing elementary theoretical generalizations as well as many paradigm methods and applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is overlap between old and new paradigms in solvable problems, but decisive differences exist in modes of solution; Kuhn uses gestalt and 'picking up the other end of the stick' metaphors to describe the conceptual reconfiguration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extraordinary research strategies during crisis
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientists in crisis isolate anomalies more precisely, magnify breakdowns, push the rules of normal science harder, perform exploratory/random experiments, and generate speculative theories to find a new paradigm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Kepler and Priestley's random-seeming investigations; twentieth-century particle and field experiments (neutrino detection, parity non-conservation) attempting to localize anomalies; such work often looks like searching at random but aims to structure the anomaly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophical analysis and thought experiments as crisis tools
rubrics_metrics.description: During crisis, philosophical analysis and thought experiments are used as devices for exposing assumptions, isolating the root of crisis, and suggesting new frameworks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kuhn notes that Newtonian, relativistic, and quantum revolutions were accompanied by philosophical analysis; thought experiments (Galileo, Einstein, Bohr) play critical roles in isolating conceptual issues that are hard to reach experimentally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crisis often produces new discoveries by concentrating attention
rubrics_metrics.description: By concentrating attention on a narrow area of trouble and preparing minds to recognize anomalies, crisis often proliferates new discoveries—some accidental, some predicted by emerging hypotheses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Lavoisier’s oxygen work, multiple optical discoveries preceding the wave theory; some discoveries convert into paradigm-supporting confirmations, others are assimilated only after re-interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: New paradigms often originate from newcomers or the young
rubrics_metrics.description: Almost always the men who achieve fundamental inventions of a new paradigm have been either very young or very new to the field whose paradigm they change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Being less committed by prior practice to traditional rules makes them likelier to see the insufficiency of existing rules and to conceive replacements; sometimes new paradigms already exist in embryo before crisis is widely recognized.
